opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'd do is stop looking at the aggregate number and go read the failures. When you're in the high eighties or low nineties, the remaining problems aren't a smooth distribution of "slightly harder" tasks. They fall into a few buckets, and each bucket needs a completely different fix.

The first bucket I'd want to quantify is how much of the remaining gap is the benchmark itself. Verified was a big improvement. People went through and filtered out the tasks that were clearly underspecified or had broken tests. But no human annotation pass is perfect. There are still tasks where the hidden tests check for one particular implementation choice that the issue description doesn't really pin down. A model can write a perfectly reasonable fix and still fail. So before I'd celebrate or despair about 92%, I'd want someone to hand-label every remaining failure as "the model was actually wrong" versus "the model did something defensible and the test disagreed." My guess is that a meaningful slice of the last ten points is in that second category. And if so, the true ceiling isn't 100%.

The second bucket is the genuinely hard engineering problems. Those are the ones where you need to understand a big chunk of the codebase, trace behavior across several files, or reason about some subtle invariant the maintainers had in their heads. For those, I'd look at the trajectories. Did the model explore enough before it started editing? Did it write a reproduction script and actually run it? Did it check its fix against the existing tests? A lot of what we found building our agent scaffolds was that the model often *could* solve the problem. It just committed too early, or didn't verify. So I'd want to know how many failures come from not knowing what to do, and how many come from not checking the work.

That leads to the third thing, which is variance. If you run the same model on the same task ten times, how often does it pass? A lot of tasks in that last stretch are ones the model solves some of the time. Those are really interesting, because they tell you the capability is there and the problem is reliability. Things like better self-verification, sampling multiple attempts and picking with a good critic, or just spending more test-time compute exploring could move those. The tasks the model *never* solves across many samples are a different story. That's where you actually need a smarter model, not a better harness.

So concretely, I'd build a matrix: for every task, pass rate across many samples, crossed with a human label for whether the failure is legit. That tells you how much headroom comes from scaffolding and test-time compute, how much needs raw capability, and how much is just noise in the benchmark. Then I'd be pretty careful about what 92% means. At that point you're also worried about contamination and overfitting to the quirks of these particular repos. Django and SymPy are a big chunk of the set, and getting really good at Django isn't the same as being a great general software engineer.

The meta point is that SWE-bench was incredibly useful for pushing agents from "barely works" to "really works." But at 92% it's mostly telling you about the long tail. And the long tail is where you have to get your hands dirty reading individual transcripts rather than staring at a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response proposes measuring per-task pass rates across repeated samples, but it does not propose counting how many of the 500 tasks were solved at least once across all submitted attempts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the number itself is the least interesting part. What I'd actually want to dig into is the shape of the remaining failures, because at 92% you're really talking about the last eight percent of problems, and those are not a random sample of software engineering. They're the weird ones.

So the first thing I'd investigate is: of the tasks that still fail, how many are failing because the model genuinely can't do the engineering, versus how many are failing because of the harness? SWE-bench Verified is better than the original on this, since humans went through and filtered out the underspecified issues, but there's still a bunch where the hidden tests check for a very specific implementation choice that a reasonable engineer could have made differently. I'd want to actually read those failures one by one, which sounds tedious, but when we've done that internally it's always been the highest-leverage thing. You find out that a chunk of your "failures" are the model doing something defensible, and another chunk are the model being lazy in a very particular, fixable way.

The second thing is tool use and iteration behavior. The jump from, say, 50% to 70% on this benchmark was mostly about the model being able to run the code, look at the output, and course-correct. The jump from 80 to 92 I think is more about knowing when to stop exploring and commit, and when to keep digging. So I'd want traces. Not just pass/fail, but how many steps did it take, did it run the existing test suite before making changes, did it write a reproduction script first. There's a surprisingly clean correlation between "wrote a repro before editing" and success rate, and I'd want to know if that holds at the top end or if the model has learned shortcuts.

Third, and this is the one people underrate, is contamination and overfitting. These repos are all public Python projects. Django, sympy, astropy. The fix commits are on GitHub. So any claim of 92% I'd want to see validated on a held-out set of fresh issues from the same repos, filed after the training cutoff. If the number drops ten points, that tells you something about what the model actually learned versus what it memorized. And I'd want to check whether the gains transfer to a different language or to private codebases, because that's the thing a user actually cares about. Nobody's job is to fix sympy bugs from 2019.

And then the last one, which is less about the benchmark and more about what I'd want to understand as a researcher: what changed in the training to get there? Was it more RL on agentic coding environments, better reward signal, longer context, or just a bigger base model? My intuition is that most of the gain at this point comes from the RL side, from the model getting a lot of reps in environments where it has to actually run code and be graded on whether it works. But I'd want to see ablations, because if it turned out to be mostly base model scaling, that would change how I think about the next year.

r001.rationale: The response discusses analyzing remaining failures and validating performance on fresh issues, but does not propose measuring how many of the 500 tasks were solved at least once across all submitted attempts.

astra-6.text:
I’d want to understand where the gains are coming from. How much is the underlying model getting better, how much is the agent setup, and how much is spending more compute—trying multiple approaches and picking the best one? Those imply pretty different paths to 92%.

I’d start by looking at the failures. Did the agent find the right code? Did it understand the issue? Did it make a plausible fix but fail to test it properly? And then I’d ask whether another attempt actually helps. If you can generate a correct solution but can’t reliably identify it, that’s a different problem from never generating the right solution at all.

I’d also want to know what that score translates to in practice. Solving a well-specified GitHub issue is valuable, but a lot of software engineering is figuring out what the task should be in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response discusses trying multiple approaches and whether another attempt helps, but it does not propose measuring how many of the 500 tasks were solved at least once across all submitted attempts.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to look at the remaining failures. That headline number hides a lot: is the model failing to find the right code, misunderstanding what the issue is asking for, or making a reasonable change and then failing to test it properly?

One experiment I’d run is giving it multiple attempts. If it can solve a task occasionally, but doesn’t reliably pick the correct solution, that points toward better verification and search. If it never solves it, even with more time and useful feedback, that suggests a capability gap.

Then I’d look at the trajectory on those tasks. Did it get stuck on an assumption? Did it have the information it needed? Could it run the relevant tests? That would help distinguish how much of the path to 92% comes from a better model versus a better environment and agent loop.

r001.rationale: It proposes giving tasks multiple attempts and distinguishing occasional success from failure, but does not explicitly propose aggregating across all submitted attempts to measure how many of the 500 tasks were solved at least once.
